title: Existence of public-key encryption
formal: Do there exist uniform classical probabilistic polynomial-time algorithms Gen, Enc and Dec forming a public-key encryption scheme for one-bit messages with negligible correctness error and IND-CPA security against every uniform classical probabilistic polynomial-time adversary, with these properties proved without an unproved hardness assumption?
why: Would establish the existence of secure public communication from a mathematical theorem rather than a computational assumption.

progress.text: Goldreich gives precise encryption security definitions, conditional constructions and relations to one-way functions.
Regev constructs classical public-key encryption under learning-with-errors hardness.
Lu and coauthors obtain classical public-key encryption from assumed average-case hardness of stabilizer decoding.

definitions: For security parameter \(n\ge 1, Gen(1^{n})\) samples a public key pk and a secret key sk. \(Enc(1^{n},pk,m)\) takes a bit \(m\in \{0,1\}\) and fresh independent coins and outputs a binary ciphertext; \(Dec(1^{n},sk,c)\) returns a bit or failure. All three algorithms have worst-case polynomial running time in their input length. Correctness means that max over \(m\in \{0,1\}\) of Pr[Dec(\(1^{n},sk,Enc(1^{n},pk,m)\))≠m] is negligible in n, with probability over key generation, encryption and any decryption coins. For IND-CPA, Gen runs first, and a uniform PPT adversary \(A_{1}\) receives \((1^{n},pk)\) and outputs bits \(m_{0},m_{1}\) and a state z. Independently choose a uniform bit b, generate \(c=Enc(1^{n},pk,m_{b})\), and give \((1^{n},pk,z,c)\) to its second stage \(A_{2}\), which outputs a bit \(b'\). For every pair \((A_{1},A_{2}), |\Pr [b' =b]- 1/2|\) must be negligible. A function \(\eta (n)\) is negligible if, for every integer \(d\ge 1, \eta (n)\le n^{- d}\) for all sufficiently large n. Adversaries may run the public encryption algorithm themselves polynomially many times before and after seeing c; there is no decryption oracle. The model has no trusted correlated setup, ideal oracle, secret advice or quantum algorithms. The receiver’s public key is given authentically; its replacement by an active attacker is outside this confidentiality experiment. One-bit message space fixes an equivalent existence question: independent bit encryptions and the standard hybrid argument extend IND-CPA security to every polynomial message length.
answer_criterion: A positive resolution proves existence of a scheme satisfying the stated correctness and computational indistinguishability bounds with no unproved computational assumption. A negative resolution proves that every efficient correct scheme fails that security requirement. An assumed-hardness construction, experimental resistance to attacks, or an impossibility theorem only for unbounded attackers does not settle this question.

context_blocks.title: Public information, private recovery
context_blocks.text: A sender receives the public key and can encrypt a message without knowing the secret key. The receiver can decrypt with that secret key. An observer has the same public encryption capability as the sender, so secrecy must come from a limitation on computation rather than from hiding the encryption algorithm. The question asks whether such a limitation can be proved to exist for some efficient scheme.

context_blocks.title: Why the challenge compares two messages
context_blocks.text: The adversary chooses two messages after seeing the public key, then receives an encryption of a fair random choice between them. Guessing always gives success \(1/2\). Security requires every efficient adversary’s additional advantage to be negligible. This is stronger than merely failing to recover a long message exactly: learning one distinguishing bit can already violate the requirement. Restricting the displayed experiment to message bits keeps the existence question concrete without requiring a particular practical ciphertext format.

context_blocks.title: A simple failure of deterministic encryption
context_blocks.text: Imagine that encryption uses no fresh randomness and the two possible messages are 0 and 1. Anyone with the public key can compute both ciphertexts and compare the challenge with them. On keys for which both messages decrypt correctly, the two ciphertexts must differ, so the comparison reveals the challenge bit. Randomized encryption avoids this immediate comparison attack, but randomness by itself is not a proof of security.

context_blocks.title: Which assumptions are still missing?
context_blocks.text: Regev’s lattice-based construction gives classical public-key encryption from learning-with-errors hardness. This is a theorem relating two computational tasks; it does not prove the assumed task hard. In March 2026, Lu, Poremba, Quek and Ramkumar gave another conditional route based on average-case hardness of quantum stabilizer decoding, with classical cryptographic algorithms. A new candidate assumption broadens the foundations available for constructions while leaving unconditional existence unresolved. The word quantum in the underlying decoding problem does not itself make the encryption algorithms quantum.

context_blocks.title: The boundary of the question
context_blocks.text: Secure public-key encryption implies one-way functions and hence \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\). The converse implication from arbitrary one-way functions is a separate open question, TCS-6545; proving that implication alone would still leave their existence unproved. Computational security here permits an unbounded adversary to succeed. Consequently, the impossibility of information-theoretic secrecy from only public information does not answer the present question. Chosen-ciphertext security adds access to a decryption oracle and is also a different requirement. The requested theorem concerns precisely efficient classical attackers in the stated chosen-plaintext experiment.

sentences: Can public-key encryption be proved computationally secure without an unproved hardness assumption?
An efficient correct scheme with negligible IND-CPA advantage against every uniform classical PPT adversary, or a proof that none exists.
Constructions from lattice and other hardness assumptions are known.
